name: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12

lead: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12, sold as Biopeptide EL, is a lab-made peptide based on a repeating elastin sequence and linked to a fatty acid. It is added to anti-aging creams so skin feels firmer and more elastic, with a smoother, younger look.

It is marketed as supporting skin elasticity. A 2025 laboratory study using label-free imaging examined its short-term effects on human skin composition and mechanics, describing it as a self-assembling peptide that interacts with skin components and may alter skin mechanics. No clinical trial results were found.

paras: It is used in daily anti-aging creams and serums, often with other peptides and moisturisers. Firmness effects from such products are generally judged over weeks of regular use.
No ingredient-specific harms were found, and safety frameworks for cosmetic peptides are still evolving. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 (Biopeptide EL) is an elastin-derived peptide in anti-aging creams, used for firmer, more elastic skin and a smoother look. It is marketed as supporting skin elasticity. A 2025 imaging study in the lab examined its effects on skin composition and mechanics.

lead: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12, sold as Biopeptide EL, is a synthetic fatty-acid-linked peptide derived from a repeating elastin sequence and used in anti-aging creams. People apply products containing it aiming for firmer, more elastic-looking skin and a smoother appearance of fine lines.

It belongs to the family of cosmetic signal peptides, which includes palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), a five-amino-acid peptide attached to a 16-carbon fatty chain that the manufacturer Sederma launched in 2000.[1] The fatty chain is described as helping such molecules enter skin lipids.[1]

A 2025 laboratory study using label-free imaging techniques tracked the peptide in full-thickness human skin, found it permeated the stratum corneum and epidermis while forming a gel, and reported that it strengthened and repaired the skin barrier after lipid removal in tests.[2] No clinical trial results were found.

paras: The peptide is promoted in anti-aging products for firmness and elasticity. Researchers describe cosmetic self-assembling peptides of this kind as interacting with skin structures, though their short-term impact on composition and mechanics had been unclear before the 2025 study.[2]

The wider category of palmitoyl matrikine peptides is described as messenger peptides said to activate genes involved in extracellular matrix renewal, an explanation Wikipedia flags as needing citation for Matrixyl.[1]

In the 2025 study, orbital trapping secondary ion mass spectrometry distinguished the peptide's sol and gel forms and tracked its self-assembly and penetration, and stimulated Raman scattering and mechanical testing showed barrier strengthening after delipidation, with co-assembly with native skin molecules shown in vitro and in ex vivo histology.[2] The authors describe the work as a methodological benchmark for measuring cosmetic peptide effects on skin mechanics.[2]
A T Nation member asking about peptides to improve healing times, scarring and results listed TB-500, GHK, Biopeptide EL and Matrixyl together as options.[3]

No studies found in human clinical trials. A 2025 ex vivo study monitored the peptide in human skin layers with non-invasive techniques and assessed its mechanical interaction with skin components.[2]

A 2026 paper proposes a bioinformatic framework for safety evaluation of cosmetic peptides as the industry shifts away from animal testing; it tested palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 along with other cosmetic peptides, and the framework correctly flagged toxin peptides such as amanitin and conotoxin in the same test set.[4] No ingredient-specific adverse-effect data were found.
